title: Using cases and precedent
summary: A case explains a court’s resolution of a dispute under particular law and facts. Its usefulness depends on the issue decided, the governing jurisdiction, and the procedural posture.
notes:
Extract the rule together with the facts that make it operate. A court may decide only that a claim can proceed, leaving facts for trial. A remand for findings is different from a final decision that a disputed contract term applies. The same opinion may discuss another rule without adopting it. Northrop makes this especially visible: the court preferred one treatment of different terms but predicted that Illinois would use another.

A statute can also change the legal landscape reflected in an older opinion. The casebook’s medical-promise notes illustrate legislative responses to judicial decisions. The Restatement provides a useful organization and persuasive formulation, but the court’s actual adoption or rejection of that formulation matters. Editorial follow-up so that a useful comparison does not silently become a claim of controlling authority.

textbookImport.basis: Plain-language synthesis of the cited casebook passages; subject to the jurisdictional and source limits stated there.

topics.precedent: The court’s chosen rule must be distinguished from commentary and alternative reasoning.
